manual.name: Eternal Spinner
manual.blurb: Spins heroically while promising the app is definitely not frozen. Definitely.
manual.note: A loading spinner signals an asynchronous task waiting on disk, network, or a slow main thread.

manual.name: Recycle Goblin
manual.blurb: Politely holds onto deleted files until you finally click Empty — and immediately regret it.
manual.note: Deleting a file usually just unlinks its directory entry until the space is overwritten.

manual.name: Small Ben
manual.blurb: A stubbornly punctual timepiece that follows you down the stack — until Ring −2 stops its hands cold.
manual.note: Computers maintain clocks at every layer: wall-clock UI, cron schedulers, and hardware timers.

manual.name: Sky Sprite
manual.blurb: Glides lazily over sunlit app windows and perches on anything with a flat titlebar.
manual.note: Represents lightweight UI animations and foreground events fluttering above the stack.

manual.name: The Collector
manual.blurb: Patrols the runtime cavern sweeping up unreachable objects with ruthless tidiness.
manual.note: Mark-and-sweep garbage collectors find live objects and reclaim everything nobody points to.

manual.name: Frame Runner
manual.blurb: Piles neatly onto its neighbors every time a function calls another function.
manual.note: Each stack frame stores a function’s local variables and where to return when it finishes.

manual.name: Heap Hopper
manual.blurb: Never flies — strictly hops from one allocated object top to the next.
manual.note: A friendly metaphor for tracing garbage-collector workers hopping across live heap references.

manual.name: Card Catalogue
manual.blurb: Dozens of tiny wooden drawers, each pointing to an exact function buried in the stacks.
manual.note: Linkers look up exported symbol tables just like a library card catalogue.

manual.name: Archivist’s Inkwell
manual.blurb: Fresh ink for the quiet clerks who maintain the standard library’s ancient indexes.
manual.note: Standard libraries bundle battle-tested helpers so every programmer doesn’t reinvent sorting.

manual.name: The Hourglass
manual.blurb: Measures quiet study in Libraries, guest CPU quotas in Ring −1, and frozen sand in Ring −2.
manual.note: Schedulers and hypervisors slice time into tiny grains so no single program hogs the CPU.

manual.name: Bookworm Blob
manual.blurb: A quiet scholar that hops softly between bookshelves and pauses to read footnotes.
manual.note: Shared libraries are like reference books every program borrows instead of rewriting from scratch.

manual.name: Small Ben

manual.note: Computers maintain clocks at every layer: wall-clock UI, cron schedulers, and hardware timers.

manual.name: Daemon Postbox
manual.blurb: Keeps its little red flag up whenever a background process has unread mail.
manual.note: Processes talk to each other through pipes, sockets, and message queues.

manual.name: Lock Ness
manual.blurb: Keeps resurfacing deeper and deeper in the machine, shedding color until only pure 1-bit steel remains.
manual.note: From file locks to hardware-sealed SMRAM, computing is locks all the way down.

manual.name: Horned Daemon
manual.blurb: Patrols the midnight skyline with brisk, tireless footsteps and tiny glowing eyes.
manual.note: In Unix, a daemon is a background service (like cron or sshd) that quietly runs without a terminal.

manual.name: Boiler Core
manual.blurb: Glows red-hot beneath the giant cogs, turning raw clock ticks into scheduled work.
manual.note: The kernel sits at Ring 0 with unrestricted access to memory, CPU cores, and hardware.

manual.name: The Watchdog
manual.blurb: Patiently counts down in the dark — if software forgets to pet it, it barks and resets the machine.
manual.note: Hardware watchdog timers recover frozen systems automatically by triggering a hard reset on timeout.

manual.name: Thread-Bot
manual.blurb: Zips in short bursts, yields politely on a gear, then sprints off on its next time slice.
manual.note: OS kernels juggle hundreds of threads by giving each one a tiny burst (quantum) of CPU time.

manual.name: Interrupt Flag
manual.blurb: Crackles with raw white lightning whenever a peripheral demands the CPU drop everything right now.
manual.note: Hardware interrupts (IRQs) let keyboards, disks, and network cards tap the CPU on the shoulder.

manual.name: Silicon Heart
manual.blurb: Starts as a humble bus chip, grows a quartz UV window in Firmware, and reveals the hidden Management Engine at the bottom.
manual.note: Modern PCs contain a tiny independent processor inside the chipset that runs even when the OS is off.

manual.name: Whirlwind
manual.blurb: Twin high-RPM fans on the graphics bus, and a solitary green-phosphor guardian inside the BIOS vault.
manual.note: Every bit flipped generates a tiny puff of heat — cooling fans keep silicon below thermal throttle.

manual.name: Wave Watcher
manual.blurb: Hums quietly on the workbench, drawing a crisp cyan sine wave that never misses a beat.
manual.note: Hardware engineers use oscilloscopes to see real voltage waves on circuit-board pins.

manual.name: Bus-Beetle
manual.blurb: Scuttles at ludicrous speed along cyan and magenta motherboard traces.
manual.note: Hardware buses shuttle millions of tiny electrical packets per second between devices and RAM.

manual.name: Vault Keeper
manual.blurb: A colossal circular bank door that sends out slow phosphor ripples as its dial turns.
manual.note: Write-protected boot flash prevents malware from silently rewriting your motherboard’s startup code.

manual.name: Save Icon Relic
manual.blurb: Younger users swear someone 3D-printed the Save icon and hid it in the BIOS vault.
manual.note: For decades, 3.5-inch floppy disks booted machines and flashed BIOS updates.

manual.blurb: A skeleton key that unlocks boot ROMs in Firmware and reappears as bare 1-bit teeth in Ring −3.
manual.note: Cryptographic root keys burned into hardware fuses verify that firmware hasn’t been tampered with.

manual.blurb: Drifts in rigid, metronomic sweeps — never jumps, never lands, never blinks out of rhythm.
manual.note: Firmware runs hardware self-tests (POST) with strict timing before an operating system even wakes up.

manual.name: The Twin Masks
manual.blurb: Host on the left, mirrored Guest on the right — swapping faces every VM exit.
manual.note: A VMCS (Virtual Machine Control Structure) saves and restores CPU state between host and guest.

manual.name: All-Seeing Lens
manual.blurb: Glances left and right across virtual memory, catching every guest page fault before it lands.
manual.note: Hypervisors intercept guest memory tables so VMs stay safely isolated from one another.

manual.name: Stopped Metronome
manual.blurb: Caught leaning right at the peak of its swing — waiting for an RSM instruction that never comes.
manual.note: Ring −2 (SMM) is invisible to the OS; when it pauses execution, time literally stands still above it.

manual.name: Suspended Splash
manual.blurb: A single teardrop hovering forever over a crown of silver pixels.
manual.note: System Management Mode suspends all normal threads in place without them ever knowing they paused.

manual.name: Frozen Ghost
manual.blurb: Caught mid-flight when System Management Mode stopped the clock. It never moves a pixel.
manual.note: When an SMI fires, the entire OS and hypervisor freeze instantaneously until SMM finishes.

manual.note: Every app, OS, and game in existence ultimately boils down to billions of microscopic transistors.

manual.blurb: Broadcasts silent 1-bit pings from the bottom of the silicon die, even when the machine is asleep.
manual.note: Out-of-band management engines can answer network pings while the main CPU is powered down.

manual.name: Bit-Mote
manual.blurb: Steps strictly along invisible 4-pixel silicon rails, flickering between pure 0 and pure 1.
manual.note: At the deepest management core, everything reduces to raw 1-bit logic pulses on bare silicon.
